turns.t: Hi, sorry, I'm Becky, Oliver's mum, and this is Gran, who has him after school. It's his bowels, he's not been going.
Hello both, hello Oliver. How old are you, Oliver? ~
Six and a half. ~
Six and a half, brilliant. Becky, how long has he been bunged up?
I'd say a couple of weeks, but Gran has him most days, so she'd know better.
Oh, I couldn't say, love. He's been like it a while, months, maybe longer. I didn't write it down.
That's fine, I'll treat it as an on-and-off problem for a while. What are the poos like when they do come?
Hard little pellets, then once a big one that blocks the toilet.
Oliver, does it hurt when you do a poo?
No. It doesn't hurt.
He screams on the toilet, doctor. He holds on to the door and goes red in the face.
He does, I've heard it from the kitchen.
I'll write down both what you've said, Oliver, and what Mum and Gran have noticed. Does your tummy hurt at other times?
Sometimes. Not now. ~
Has he ever had an operation, Becky?
A hernia repair, when he was two.
Any other health problems?
Eczema, but it's much better.
Okay. I'm going to feel your tummy, Oliver. Lie down on the bed. ~
It tickles. ~
His tummy is soft, but I can feel hard lumps low down on the left, which is stool.
Is that normal? ~
It tells me the bowel is full. Nothing else looks worrying. His bottom looks normal, no cracks.
Can you see the problem? ~
Weight 21 kilos, which is right for his age.
So what's going on? ~
Most likely this is functional constipation, which is very common. I can't rule out an underactive thyroid, but it's less likely.
What do we do about it? ~
First, no medicine today. I'd like you to try more fibre, more water, and regular toilet sits after meals for four weeks, with a sticker chart.
I can do stickers at mine. ~
Please do. Don't tell him off about accidents. ~
And if it's no better? ~
I'll see you again in four weeks, and we'll think about treatment.
Four weeks. Thanks, doctor. ~
Can I have a sticker now? ~
Absolutely. ~
